newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Nestle rejects Greenpeace soybean protest.
newsitem.headline: Nestle rejects Greenpeace soybean protest.

text.p: Greenpeace demonstrators fighting the use of genetically altered soybeans in food draped a protest banner from Nestle SA's headquarters in Switzerland on Monday before being dispersed by police.
"Gene food: Force fed by Nestle" said the banner spread out by a handful of environmentalist activists who swung from ropes from the roof at the world's largest food company.
Some three dozen activists called on Nestle to distance itself from genetically engineered soybeans, which they call a risky experiment with nature that could endanger human health.
Nestle shrugged off the protest and insisted the products were safe.

"We are singularly unimpressed with the scientific evidence presented by Greenpeace and we continue to be convinced that these products are safe and of high quality," company spokesman Francois Perroud told Reuters.
"Therefore Nestle will use genetically modified soybeans in its products."
Perroud said Nestle was not worried that consumers alerted by recent Greenpeace protests in Europe would reject genetically altered soybeans.

"Experience with other genetically modified products shows that once the product is in use, this consumer concern -- which is entirely artificial and entirely fostered by a small number of activists -- will subside very quickly," he said.
A new variety of genetically altered soybean developed by Monsanto Co is resistant to its Roundup herbicide. Authorities in the U.S. and Europe have approved it.
Every week in Europe thousands of tonnes of soybeans are processed into meal and oil, which is used in a wide variety of everyday foods such as margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.

But some leading European firms, including the German units of Nestle and Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have bowed to consumer pressure and announced they will not use the new variety of soybean even though they consider it safe.
Leading chocolate company Kraft Jacobs Suchard SA said on Friday it would not use the new soybeans in its European products for now, but was not opposed to the bean in principle on safety grounds.
Perroud left open whether Nestle's German unit would reverse course at some stage.
"Germany for the time being does not use these beans," he said.
